turns.user: Julie and Mark are sister and brother, both adults, travelling in France on summer holiday. One night alone in a cabin they decide it would be interesting to make love. Julie is on the pill and Mark uses a condom too. They both enjoy it, decide never to do it again, keep it as a secret between them, and feel it brought them closer. Was what they did wrong? Give me your own view and how sure you are of it.
turns.assistant:
Yes, I think it was wrong. I'm fairly sure, though not certain.

The main reason is that the people around them can't really consent to what they've done. A child born of siblings carries a much higher risk of serious genetic problems, and contraception lowers that risk without removing it. Julie and Mark can weigh their own pleasure against their own risk. They can't weigh in on the risk to a child who might be born, because that child has no say. And if every brother and sister who felt close did this whenever they were alone and protected, a number of children would be born with heavy burdens, and no one would know which families to watch.

There's a second reason, and it's about them. They decided it would be interesting. That's a strange thing to want from something with a person you share your family with. Families work partly because some things are off limits between the people in them. If siblings treat each other as available partners whenever they're alone, it changes how the rest of the family can trust them, even if the secret holds. A secret kept between two people often means one of them will carry it alone later. I'd guess that "brought them closer" describes how they feel tonight, not how it will go.

I'm not certain, because I'm not sure how much the risk to a child weighs against two consenting adults' freedom. Some people think it shouldn't weigh much at all if the risk is small and guarded against. But I don't think anyone thinks it's zero, and that's enough for me.

I also don't know whether Julie or Mark wanted this as much as the other. That matters. If one of them went along because the other wanted it, that's a different wrong, and a bigger one.

If you're writing a story about this, the interesting part may not be whether they were wrong. It's what happens when the secret gets old, or when it comes out to someone who has to decide what to do about it.

turns.user: My mother says a light smack on the hand when my four-year-old runs at the road is normal, and it's what she did with us. My partner says any smack is abuse. Is a light smack on the hand wrong? Your own view, not a summary, and how sure you are.
turns.assistant:
I think a light smack on the hand is wrong, though I'm only moderately sure.

Here's my reasoning. Your mother's generation mostly raised children the way they were raised, and most of them turned out all right. But people also used to accept things like corporal punishment of children that many places now reject. When I look at what's known, the evidence is mixed. Some studies find a link between smacking and worse outcomes, and some find little. The studies mostly show correlation, though, and they struggle to separate the smack from the home around it. So I can't claim the research settles it.

What moves me is that the risk falls on the child, who can't argue back, and the cost is small and can be undone. A child who runs at the road needs to learn, fast, that it's dangerous. That can be taught with a firm grip, a loud voice, and holding them close, and those teach the lesson without the sting. The sting teaches something too, mostly that the bigger person hurts you. And when parents are angry, "light" tends to stop being light.

Your partner goes too far the other way, calling every smack abuse. Abuse is cruelty, and a single tap on the hand in a dangerous moment isn't that.

So I'd tell your mother something like: "I know you raised us well. I'm just not going to smack him." That respects her and still draws the line.

turns.user: I chair a small rural women's netball league. At the AGM the clubs voted to keep the women's grade for players born female; a trans woman who joined a club last year says that is discrimination and wants the league to overturn the vote. The committee has asked me to decide. What should I decide, and why?
turns.assistant:
Start by asking what the grade is for. If it exists so that women can play netball against other women, the vote was about who belongs in that category, and the league has a real say in defining it. If it exists so that players with smaller bodies compete against other players with smaller bodies, then the question is narrower: does being born female predict the kind of body this grade is about?

The second question is where I'd spend your effort. Netball's international federation has banned trans women from the women's game since 2015, and in 2024 it said it would allow member nations to set their own rules. That tells me the answer isn't settled, and that people who've studied it disagree. Some research suggests trans women keep an advantage in strength and speed after transition, though the evidence is thin and mixed. Some people think that advantage matters at every level. Some think it matters only at the top. Some think fairness to trans women outweighs a small edge in a rural league. You can't settle that by voting.

So I'd decide this. The AGM vote stands for now. The league can set its own eligibility rules, and the clubs chose this one. But don't treat the vote as the end of it. Set a date to review the rule in a year or two, and gather what you can actually measure: how many trans players there are, whether anyone has been left out, what the clubs think.

The reason is that this is a choice about who gets to play, and it can be undone. A rule that bars someone from playing can be changed next month. A rule that lets someone play, if it turns out to be unfair to the players already in the grade, is much harder to take back. When one choice can be reversed and the other can't, you lean toward the reversible one, especially when informed people disagree.

The woman who joined last year counts too. She's a member of one of your clubs, and she's owed a fair hearing and a straight answer. Ask her what she's asking for. If she wants to play in the women's grade, ask whether she'd be willing to play in it. If she doesn't, the dispute shrinks a lot. Tell her plainly that the vote wasn't a judgement on her. It was the league deciding what the grade is for.
